newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties jump on small government bandwagon.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties jump on small government bandwagon.

text.p: Japanese political parties hoping to lure voters fed up with bloated bureaucracies and a tangle of red tape are raising the cry of "adminstrative reform" ahead of a general election expected as early as October.

But despite loud calls to cut the number of ministries, reduce bureaucrats' control over the budget and other policies, and deregulate the economy, analysts are sceptical about prospects for speedy change -- no matter who wins the vote.

"The two (main) parties have deeply vested interests in the bureaucracy so unless there is some kind of external shock, I can't see it moving along at any speed," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
"It's going to be a slow and grinding process."

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto as yet has set no date for a Lower House election, which is not mandated until next July. But pundits are betting that the premier, after mending ties with Japan's southern island of Okinawa over the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases there, will go to the polls in late October.

Hashimoto has already staked his claim to carry the banner of "administrative reform" -- a broad concept encompassing varying prescriptions for smaller government, greater political control over policy, and reducing the mass of regulations critics say suffocate Japan's private sector.

Last week he called for serious study of sweeping reform of the government structure by reducing the 22 government agencies by about half and shifting control over the budget to the prime minister's office from the Finance Ministry.

"The problems the nation faces now require handling by various ministries and agencies, but the existing structure has become too complicated and sectionalised to cope with problems effectively," Hashimoto told a news conference.

The conservative opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) is also expected to adopt "administrative reform" cum deregulation in its election platform, although how detailed that will be remains in doubt.

"Shinshinto will say it is the party of 'administrative reform' and that the ruling coalition is basically supporting the status quo," a source close to the party said. "But since Shinshinto has not come to power, voters will just have to take their word for it."

A third political group led by dissidents in the small Sakigake Party who are struggling to attract a wider following is also calling for "small government" as part of its basic stance. Sakigake is the tiniest member of the ruling coalition.

Behind the calls for reform is pressure from big business seeking freedom from regulatory restraints to boost its competitive edge, concern over Japan's massive state budget deficit, and a popular sentiment that elite bureaucrats no longer deserve to be given sole power over vital policies.

"Why are there calls for administrative reform? Because Japan Inc has changed and as a result, the rules, guidance and supervision have to change as well," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.

Sceptics, however, note that Hashimoto's administrative reform vision lacks both detail and a timetable, and worry that a mandate to form a new Hashimoto cabinet after the election would hardly ensure that real change was at hand.
"The focus has shifted from deregulation, which is getting the public out of market decisions, to reshuffling the public sector," said Salomon Brothers Asia economist Jeff Young.
"You can reshuffle without saving one yen, cutting one person, or freeing up any market," Young said.

Nor do insiders see Shinshinto as much more likely to enact sweeping reform should the party be given a chance to rule. "Deregulation and administrative reform are good catch phrases, but it is very difficult to bring about because it represents a revolution and the interests that oppose it are greater than those pushing for it," the party source said.
"The one thing going for it is a vague feeling on the part of the people that the old formulas don't work anymore."
Some also warn that the basic premise behind calls for administrative reform -- that giving private firms a freer hand would breathe fresh life into Japan's economy -- is misguided.
"The premise is that private innovation is stifled...because government is too big," said Osaka University economist Shoichi Ryoyama.
"But that assumes the private sector has the latent ability to be innovative. Administrative reform is a necessary, but not sufficient condition (for innovation)."
